### 2 Partial Wannierization

We first investigate the band topology in the case shown in Fig. S1(a), in which the top two moiré bands have the same valley Chern number $\mathcal{C}=(-1,-1)$ . The $C_{3z}$ eigenvalues of the top two moiré bands cannot be written as the summation of two elementary band representations. Therefore, they cannot be maximally Wannierized together. However, one can still notice that if we combine the Bloch state at $\gamma$ point from the second moiré band, and the Bloch states away from the $\gamma$ point from the first moiré band, then an elementary band representation $(\overline{{}^{2}E})_{1a}\uparrow P3$ can be found.

Based on this observation, the authors proposed a “partial Wannierization” procedure in Ref. [19]. Using the “disentangle” Wannierization functionality provided by Wannier90 [48, 49, 50], we are able to construct the wave function which indeed corresponds to a maximally localized orbital dubbed MLWF. Such MLWF is constructed by choosing a proper ${\mathbf{k}}$ -dependent superposition of the wave functions of the top two moiré bands:

$$ f^{\dagger}_{{\mathbf{k}},\sigma}=\sum_{n=1,2}c^{\dagger}_{{\mathbf{k}},n,\sigma}U^{\rm dis}_{n}({\mathbf{k}})=\sum_{\mathbf{Q}}\tilde{u}^{(\sigma)}_{\mathbf{Q},f}({\mathbf{k}})c^{\dagger}_{{\mathbf{k}}-\mathbf{Q},\sigma}\,, $$

in which $c^{\dagger}_{{\mathbf{k}},n,\sigma}$ stands for the creation operator of the top two moiré energy bands, and $c^{\dagger}_{{\mathbf{k}}-\mathbf{Q},\sigma}$ stands for the plane wave creation operator for the continuum model, which will also be used in Sec. D. Accordingly, the corresponding “conduction orbital” can be constructed by a Gram–Schmidt process, which will carry all the topology obstruction with total valley Chern number $\mathcal{C}=-2$ . Hence, it cannot be maximally Wannierized [51]. We further fix the gauge of this orbital using the method introduced in Ref. [52], which leads to a Wannier function that decays in a polynomial manner.

We can still define the “kinetic energy” of the $c$ orbitals, and the hybridization functions between the $f$ and $c$ orbitals. The effective Hamiltonian which captures the electronic structure of the top two moiré bands can be written as the following form:

$$ H_{t}=\sum_{\mathbf{R}\mathbf{R}^{\prime}\sigma}t_{ff}^{(\sigma)}(\mathbf{R})f^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{R}+\mathbf{R}^{\prime},\sigma}f_{\mathbf{R}^{\prime},\sigma}+\sum_{{\mathbf{k}},\sigma}\varepsilon^{(\sigma)}_{c}({\mathbf{k}})c^{\dagger}_{{\mathbf{k}},\sigma}c_{{\mathbf{k}}\,\sigma}+\sum_{{\mathbf{k}},\sigma}\left(V_{\rm hyb}^{(\sigma)}({\mathbf{k}})f^{\dagger}_{{\mathbf{k}},\sigma}c_{{\mathbf{k}},\sigma}+{\rm h.c.}\right)\,. $$

Here, we also note that the nearest neighbor hoppings among $f$ orbital is more than $5$ times larger than the next-nearest neighbor ones. Besides, since the $c$ orbitals in this model is not maximally localized, we emphasize that this Hamiltonian is not a tight-binding model in the traditional sense.

### 3 Two-orbital effective model

We also briefly describe the effective two-orbital model, that is suitable for the parameter regime shown in Fig. S1(b), in which the top two moiré bands carry the opposite valley Chern numbers $\mathcal{C}=(-1,+1)$ . The construction of the two orbital model was addressed in the supplemental material of Ref. [11]. Noticing that in Fig. S1(b), the $C_{3z}$ eigenvalues of the top two bands at high symmetry points can form two elementary band representations $(\overline{E})_{1b}\uparrow P3$ and $(\overline{E})_{1c}\uparrow P3$ (or equivalently, elementary band representations $(^{2}E)_{1b}\uparrow P3$ and $(^{2}E)_{1c}\uparrow P3$ if we consider the continuum model as a “spinless” Hamiltonian). Therefore, a tight-binding model can be constructed for the top two bands using Wannier90 [48, 49, 50] in a straightforward manner. The effective Hamiltonian can have the following form:

$$ H_{t}=\sum_{\mathbf{R}\mathbf{R}^{\prime}\sigma}\left(t_{ff}^{(\sigma)}(\mathbf{R})f^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{R}+\mathbf{R}^{\prime},\sigma}f_{\mathbf{R}^{\prime},\sigma}+t_{cc}^{(\sigma)}(\mathbf{R})c^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{R}+\mathbf{R}^{\prime},\sigma}c_{\mathbf{R}^{\prime},\sigma}+t_{fc}^{(\sigma)}f^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{R}+\mathbf{R}^{\prime},\sigma}c_{\mathbf{R}^{\prime},\sigma}+{\rm h.c.}\right)\,. $$

The values of all these hopping terms are also provided in Ref. [11]. For example, the nearest-neighbor hopping among the $f$ orbitals is given by $t^{(\uparrow)}_{ff}(\mathbf{a}_{1})=4.28e^{i118^{\circ}}\,\rm meV$ , and the nearest-neighbor hybridization between the two types of orbitals are given by $t^{(\uparrow)}_{fc}(\mathbf{0})=3.51e^{i48^{\circ}}\,\rm meV$ . The spin down components ( $\sigma=\downarrow$ ) are simply the complex conjugation of their spin up counterparts due to the time-reversal symmetry.

### 4 The limit of vanishing displacement field

The previous discussion about these two effective models are based on space group $P3$ , which possesses three-fold rotation symmetry. In fact, at zero displacement field limit, the moiré continuum model also has an extra $C_{2y}T$ symmetry. Besides, due to the over-simplification in the choice of the moiré potential, the moiré continuum model also has a “pseudo-inversion” symmetry [53].

The extra symmetries in vanishing displacement field limit imposes extra constraints to the effective model. For example, the nearest neighbor hopping of MLWF in the case with $\mathcal{C}=(-1,-1)$ is real $(t_{f}\in\mathbb{R})$ in the limit $\varepsilon_{D}=0$ . Nonetheless, the effective Kondo lattice and $t$ - $J$ model mapping are still valid in this limit, as the MLWF and TPLO are still not equivalent. In contrast, in the parameter regime with Chern numbers $\mathcal{C}=(-1,+1)$ , the two orbitals will become “degenerate”. Near the total filling factor $\nu_{h}=1$ , both orbitals will be around quarter filling instead of half filling. As a consequence, the Kondo lattice description is not suitable. Due to this reason, we limit our discussion for the two-orbital model in the presence of displacement field [see Fig. 3(f) in the main text].

## B Derivation of the Kondo lattice $t$ - $J$ model

### 1 Schrieffer-Wolff transformation

In this section, we briefly review the derivation of the effective $t$ - $J$ model from a tight-binding model. The derivation is similar to that in Ref. [31], while here we also take the spin-orbit coupling into account as in Refs. [32, 21]. The foundation of the derivation is the Schrieffer-Wolff transformation [30], which can be considered as a 2nd order perturbative expansion of a Hamiltonian in a small parameter. We start with a Hamiltonian of the form:

$$ H=H_{0}+H_{1}\,, $$

in which $H_{0}$ is the unperturbed Hamiltonian with a low-energy subspace $\mathcal{H}_{L}$ and a high-energy subspace $\mathcal{H}_{H}$ , and $H_{1}$ is the perturbation. It is usually more convenient to rewrite the Hamiltonian in the block form:

$$ H_{0}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}H_{L}&0\\
0&H_{H}\end{array}\right)\,,\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ H_{1}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&V\\
V^{\dagger}&0\end{array}\right)\,, $$

in which the matrices $H_{L}$ , $H_{H}$ are already diagonalized, and the eigenvalues of $H_{L}$ are well-separated from those of $H_{H}$ . For simplicity, we assume that the low-energy subspace is spanned by eigenstates with the same eigenvalue $\varepsilon^{L}$ , and the high-energy subspace is spanned by eigenstates with all eigenvalues satisfying $\varepsilon^{H}_{m}\geq\varepsilon^{L}$ . The Schödinger equation of this Hamiltonian is given by:

$$ \displaystyle H_{L}|\psi_{L}\rangle+V|\psi_{H}\rangle \displaystyle=E|\psi_{L}\rangle\,, \displaystyle V^{\dagger}|\psi_{L}\rangle+H_{H}|\psi_{H}\rangle \displaystyle=E|\psi_{H}\rangle\,. $$

We first solve the second equation for $|\psi_{H}\rangle$ :

$$ |\psi_{H}\rangle=\sum_{m\in\mathcal{H}_{H}}|m\rangle\frac{\langle m|V^{\dagger}|\psi_{L}\rangle}{E-\varepsilon^{H}_{m}}\,, $$

in which $|m\rangle$ stands for the eigenstates of $H_{0}$ in the high-energy subspace. Substituting this into the first equation, we have:

$$ \left[H_{L}+\sum_{m\in\mathcal{H}_{H}}\frac{V|m\rangle\langle m|V^{\dagger}}{E-\varepsilon_{m}^{H}}\right]|\psi_{L}\rangle=E|\psi_{L}\rangle\,. $$

Obviously, this equation is an effective Schödinger equation for the low-energy subspace with second order perturbation corrections from $H_{1}$ . Since the low-energy subspace is spanned by eigenstates with the same eigenvalue $\varepsilon^{L}$ , we can approximate the eigenvalue $E$ in the low-energy subspace as $E\approx\varepsilon^{L}$ . Therefore, in the low-energy subspace $n,n^{\prime}\in\mathcal{H}_{L}$ , the effective Hamiltonian is given by:

$$ [H_{\text{eff}}]_{nn^{\prime}}=\varepsilon^{L}\delta_{nn^{\prime}}+\sum_{m\in\mathcal{H}_{H}}\frac{\langle n|V|m\rangle\langle m|V^{\dagger}|n^{\prime}\rangle}{\varepsilon^{L}-\varepsilon^{H}_{m}}\,. $$

Here the second term contains the second order perturbation corrections from $H_{1}$ for the low-energy effective theory. In the following, we will apply this method to derive the effective $t$ - $J$ model from a tight-binding model with strong spin-orbit coupling.

### 2 Superexchange interaction with spin-orbit coupling

Generally, the $t$ - $J$ model is considered as a low-energy effective theory of a tight-binding model with strong Hubbard interaction. The spin-spin interactions can be derived from a Schrieffer-Wolff transformation of the above Hamiltonian at half-filling. Clearly, the low-energy subspace is spanned by the states with exactly one electron on each site, which all have eigenvalues $\varepsilon^{L}=0$ . The wave functions of these low-energy states can be written as:

$$ \mathcal{H}_{L}=\left\{\{|\sigma_{\mathbf{R}\alpha}\}\rangle=\prod_{\mathbf{R}\alpha}c^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{R}\alpha,\sigma_{\mathbf{R}\alpha}}|0\rangle\Bigg|\sigma_{\mathbf{R}\alpha}=\uparrow,\downarrow\right\}\,, $$

where $|0\rangle$ is the vacuum state. Such low-energy subspace is equivalent to the Hilbert space of a spin-1/2 system. The coupling between the spin moments on any two different sites can be derived from Schrieffer-Wolff transformation using the hopping terms as the perturbation. For simplicity, we first solve the two-site problem considering only $\mathbf{R}\alpha$ (denoted as 1) and $\mathbf{R}^{\prime}\beta$ (denoted as 2). In the low-energy subspace of two-site Hubbard model, there are four states:

$$ \displaystyle|\uparrow\uparrow\rangle= \displaystyle c^{\dagger}_{1\uparrow}c^{\dagger}_{2\uparrow}|0\rangle\,, \displaystyle|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle= \displaystyle c^{\dagger}_{1\uparrow}c^{\dagger}_{2\downarrow}|0\rangle\,, \displaystyle|\downarrow\uparrow\rangle= \displaystyle c^{\dagger}_{1\downarrow}c^{\dagger}_{2\uparrow}|0\rangle\,, \displaystyle|\downarrow\downarrow\rangle= \displaystyle c^{\dagger}_{1\downarrow}c^{\dagger}_{2\downarrow}|0\rangle\,. $$

Besides, there are two high-energy states, which will be denoted as $|20\rangle$ and $|02\rangle$ :

$$ \displaystyle|20\rangle= \displaystyle c^{\dagger}_{1\uparrow}c^{\dagger}_{1\downarrow}|0\rangle\,, \displaystyle|02\rangle= \displaystyle c^{\dagger}_{2\uparrow}c^{\dagger}_{2\downarrow}|0\rangle\,. $$

Suppose the hopping from site $2$ to site $1$ with spin $\uparrow$ is given by $t\in\mathbb{C}$ , the perturbation Hamiltonian can be written as:

$$ \displaystyle H_{0} \displaystyle=U\left(|20\rangle\langle 20|+|02\rangle\langle 02|\right)\,, \displaystyle H_{1} \displaystyle=tc^{\dagger}_{1\uparrow}c_{2\uparrow}+t^{*}c^{\dagger}_{2\uparrow}c_{1\uparrow}+tc^{\dagger}_{2\downarrow}c_{1\downarrow}+t^{*}c^{\dagger}_{1\downarrow}c_{2\downarrow}\,. $$

Using the expression in Eq. (S15), it is easy to show that only the following matrix elements in the effective Hamiltonian are non-zero:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\uparrow\downarrow|H_{\rm eff}|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle \displaystyle=-\frac{|\langle\uparrow\downarrow|H_{t}|02\rangle|^{2}}{U}-\frac{|\langle\uparrow\downarrow|H_{t}|20\rangle|^{2}}{U}=-\frac{2|t|^{2}}{U}\,, \displaystyle\langle\downarrow\uparrow|H_{\rm eff}|\downarrow\uparrow\rangle \displaystyle=-\frac{|\langle\downarrow\uparrow|H_{t}|02\rangle|^{2}}{U}-\frac{|\langle\downarrow\uparrow|H_{t}|20\rangle|^{2}}{U}=-\frac{2|t|^{2}}{U}\,, \displaystyle\langle\uparrow\downarrow|H_{\rm eff}|\downarrow\uparrow\rangle \displaystyle=-\frac{\langle\uparrow\downarrow|H_{t}|02\rangle\langle 02|H_{t}|\downarrow\uparrow\rangle}{U}-\frac{\langle\uparrow\downarrow|H_{t}|20\rangle\langle 20|H_{t}|\downarrow\uparrow\rangle}{U}=\frac{2t^{2}}{U}\,, \displaystyle\langle\downarrow\uparrow|H_{\rm eff}|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle \displaystyle=\langle\uparrow\downarrow|H_{\rm eff}|\downarrow\uparrow\rangle^{*}=\frac{2(t^{*})^{2}}{U}\,. $$

These matrix elements can be reorganized into the following form using the spin operators:

$$ \displaystyle H_{\rm eff}= \displaystyle\frac{4|t|^{2}}{U}\left[\frac{1}{2}\left(e^{i2\phi}S^{+}_{1}S^{-}_{2}+e^{-i2\phi}S^{-}_{1}S^{+}_{2}\right)+\left(S^{z}_{1}S^{z}_{2}-\frac{1}{4}\right)\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{4|t|^{2}}{U}\left[\left(S^{x}_{1}S^{x}_{2}+S^{y}_{1}S^{y}_{2}\right)\cos 2\phi+\hat{\bf z}\cdot\left(\mathbf{S}_{1}\times\mathbf{S}_{2}\right)\sin 2\phi+\left(S^{z}_{1}S^{z}_{2}-\frac{1}{4}\right)\right]\,, $$

where the phase angle in this effective spin Hamiltonian is defined as $\phi={\rm arg}\,t$ . Note that the effective spin-spin interaction can also contain a Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) term when $t^{2}$ is not a real number, explicitly breaking the $SU(2)$ symmetry.

One may also notice that the effective Hamiltonian of the two-site problem still has the energy spectrum of an $SU(2)$ symmetric Heisenberg model. This is due to a “hidden” $SU(2)$ algebra that only exists in this two-site variant of the model. We can consider the following gauge transformation for the fermionic states on the second site:

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{c}^{\dagger}_{2\uparrow} \displaystyle=c^{\dagger}_{2\uparrow}e^{-i\phi}\,, \displaystyle\tilde{c}^{\dagger}_{2\downarrow} \displaystyle=c^{\dagger}_{2\downarrow}e^{i\phi}\,. $$

Obviously, such transformation will remove the phase factor in the hopping term, and will also lead to the following transformation of the spin operator on site 2:

$$ \tilde{S}^{+}_{2}=S^{+}_{2}e^{-i2\phi}\,. $$

This is equivalent to a $2\phi$ rotation of the spin on site 2 around the $z$ -axis, and the DM interaction term will be eliminated by this transformation. Therefore, this two-site Hamiltonian will commute with the operators $\tilde{S}^{\pm}=S^{\pm}_{1}+\tilde{S}^{\pm}_{2}$ and $\tilde{S}^{z}=S_{1}^{z}+S_{2}^{z}$ , which form an $SU(2)$ algebra. However, such transformation cannot be generalized to the lattice case when the hoppings of the lattice model form closed loops. The only exception is the case when the accumulated rotation angles of the $S^{+}$ operators along any closed loops are integer multiples of $2\pi$ , which corresponds to a tight-binding model with the accumulated phase factors along any closed loops being integer multiples of $\pi$ for a given spin species. Such tight-binding model can be transformed into the form with all real hopping amplitudes by a gauge transformation, which will lead to an $SU(2)$ symmetric Hamiltonian. In generic cases, the effective Hamiltonian will contain DM terms that cannot be removed by any gauge transformation, and will only have a $U(1)$ symmetry associated with the total $S^{z}$ operator.

### 3 $t$ - $J$ model description for tWSe2

As we have already addressed in Sec. A, the top two bands of the continuum model can be well described by compact molecular orbitals, with one orbital near half-filling being more correlated. We denote this orbital as the $f$ orbital, while the more itinerant one is labeled as the $c$ band. Based on this construction, the effective Hamiltonian for nearest neighbor interactions takes the form as:

$$ \displaystyle H_{t}= \displaystyle t_{f}\sum_{\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{R}^{\prime}=\bm{\delta}_{1,2,3},\sigma}\left(e^{i\sigma\phi_{f}}f^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{R}\sigma}f_{\mathbf{R}^{\prime}\sigma}+{\rm h.c.}\right)+\sum_{{\mathbf{k}},\sigma}\varepsilon^{(\sigma)}_{c}({\mathbf{k}})c^{\dagger}_{{\mathbf{k}}\sigma}c_{{\mathbf{k}}\sigma}+\sum_{{\mathbf{k}}\sigma}\left(V^{(\sigma)}_{\rm hyb}({\mathbf{k}})f^{\dagger}_{{\mathbf{k}}\sigma}c_{{\mathbf{k}}\sigma}+{\rm h.c.}\right)\,, \displaystyle H_{J}= \displaystyle\frac{4|t_{f}|^{2}}{U}\sum_{\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{R}^{\prime}=\bm{\delta}_{1,2,3}}\left[\frac{1}{2}\left(S^{+}_{f\mathbf{R}}S^{-}_{f\mathbf{R}^{\prime}}e^{i2\phi_{f}}+S^{-}_{f\mathbf{R}}S^{+}_{f\mathbf{R}^{\prime}}e^{-i2\phi_{f}}\right)+\left(S^{z}_{f\mathbf{R}}S^{z}_{f\mathbf{R}^{\prime}}-\frac{1}{4}n_{f\mathbf{R}}n_{f\mathbf{R}^{\prime}}\right)\right]\,, $$

in which the anti-ferromagnetic correlation is only considered between the $f$ orbitals. This form is equivalent to Eqs. (2) and (3) in the main text.

## C Pairing channels, BdG Hamiltonian and Energetics of the Pairing States

In this section, we provide a more detailed description of our analysis on the superconducting states of the two effective $t$ - $J$ models discussed in the main text.

We decouple the effective interaction in the pairing channels following the approaches of Ref. [33, 34]. Accordingly, the superconducting order parameters can decompose into irreducible representations of the $C_{3}$ point group: the non-degenerate $A_{1}$ channel and the two-fold degenerate ${}^{1,2}E$ channels. The resulting Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) Hamiltonian takes the form

$$ H_{mf}=\sum_{\mathbf{k}}\Psi_{\mathbf{k}}^{\dagger}\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\mathbf{h}_{\mathbf{k}}&\mathbf{\Delta}_{\mathbf{k}}\\
\mathbf{\Delta}^{*}_{\mathbf{k}}&-\mathbf{h}_{\mathbf{k}}\end{array}\right]\Psi_{\mathbf{k}}+\sum_{\mathbf{k},j}\mathcal{E}_{\mathbf{k}j}+\frac{3N}{2J}\sum_{\Gamma}|\Delta_{\Gamma}|^{2}\,, $$

where the Nambu spinor is defined as: $\Psi^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{k}}=(f^{\dagger}_{{\mathbf{k}}\uparrow},c^{\dagger}_{{\mathbf{k}}\uparrow},f_{-{\mathbf{k}}\downarrow},c_{-{\mathbf{k}}\downarrow})$ , and $h_{\mathbf{k}}$ is the normal-state Hamiltonian in the $(f,c)$ orbital basis [19, 11]. Since pairing arises only among the localized $f$ -electrons, the pairing matrix $\mathbf{\Delta}_{\mathbf{k}}$ is nonzero solely in the $f$ -orbital sector $\mathbf{\Delta}_{\mathbf{k}}=\mathrm{diag}[\sum_{\Gamma}\Delta_{\Gamma}\gamma_{\Gamma}(\mathbf{k}),0]$ , with $\Delta_{\Gamma}=-\frac{2J}{3N}\sum_{k}\langle\gamma_{\Gamma}(\mathbf{k})f_{-\mathbf{k}\downarrow}f_{\mathbf{k}\uparrow}\rangle$ .

Before discussing the superconducting properties, we first clarify the order parameter symmetry information to build intuition about the symmetry of the pairing states. We define the spin-singlet and triplet pairing operators on the nearest-neighbor bonds of the more localized $f$ -orbital, $\Delta_{j}^{s,t}=\langle f_{i\uparrow}f_{i+\bm{\delta}_{j}\downarrow}\mp f_{i\downarrow}f_{i+\bm{\delta}_{j}\uparrow}\rangle$ , where $j=1,2,3$ labels the three nearest-neighbor bond directions $\bm{\delta}_{j}$ , and the upper (lower) sign corresponds to the singlet (triplet) channel. The pairing amplitude $\Delta_{\Gamma}$ in each irreducible representation $\Gamma=A_{1},{}^{1}E,{}^{2}E$ can then be expressed in terms of these bond pairing $\Delta_{j}^{s,t}$ as:

$$ \displaystyle\Delta_{\Gamma}= \displaystyle-\frac{J}{3}\cos{\phi_{f}}(\Delta_{1}^{s}+\omega_{\Gamma}\Delta_{2}^{s}+\omega_{\Gamma}^{2}\Delta_{3}^{s}) \displaystyle+\frac{J}{3}\sin{\phi_{f}}(\Delta_{1}^{t}+\omega_{\Gamma}\Delta_{2}^{t}+\omega_{\Gamma}^{2}\Delta_{3}^{t})\,, $$

where $\omega_{\Gamma}=1,e^{i2\pi/3},e^{i4\pi/3}$ corresponds to the basis functions of the $C_{3}$ irreducible representations. Due to the presence of strong spin-orbit coupling (SOC), spin SU(2) symmetry is explicitly broken. As a result, the superconducting order parameter is no longer constrained to be an even or odd function of ${\mathbf{k}}$ , and spin-singlet and spin-triplet components are allowed to mix within each irreducible representations of the $C_{3}$ symmetry group. In particular, in the model with valley Chern number $\mathcal{C}=(-1,-1)$ , when the displacement field vanishes ( $\phi_{f}=\pi$ in this case), the order parameter becomes an even function of ${\mathbf{k}}$ , leading to pure “spin-singlet” pairing. This is consistent with prior results on one-band $t$ - $J$ models on triangular lattices with real hoppings, where the dominant pairing channel is found to be of singlet $d_{x^{2}-y^{2}}+id_{xy}$ character. [40, 41, 42, 43, 44, 54].

To determine which pairing channel is energetically favorable, we compute the ground state energy density as a function of pairing amplitudes

$$ \displaystyle E_{g}=\sum_{{\Gamma}}\frac{3N}{2J}|\Delta_{\Gamma}|^{2}-\sum_{{\mathbf{k}},j=\pm}(E_{{\mathbf{k}},j}-\mathcal{E}_{{\mathbf{k}},j}), $$

by minimizing it with respect to each pairing amplitude $\Delta_{{\Gamma}}$ . Here $E_{{\mathbf{k}},j}$ denote the quasiparticle dispersion spectra obtained by diagonalizing the Hamiltonian $H_{mf}$ , and $\mathcal{E}_{{\mathbf{k}},j}$ is the corresponding normal-state energy. Note that the ground state energies contain the contributions from the combined $f$ and $c$ electrons. In the following, we analyze the features of the unconventional superconducting state realized in the system. Throughout this work, we scale all energies by the bandwidth evaluated at $\varepsilon_{D}=10$ meV, and the chemical potential $\mu$ is tuned to maintain half-filling unless explicitly stated otherwise. These conventions are applied consistently to both models.

## D Determination of topological index

In this section, we will discuss how we can identify the topological index of the Bogoliubov bands in both models, especially for the two-band model with the topological power-law orbital.

We start from the Kondo-lattice model with the MLWF and TPLO as the active degrees of freedom, i.e., the case with $\mathcal{C}=(-1,-1)$ . Since there is no spin-parallel pairing terms in the $t$ - $J$ model, the “creation operator” of a Bogoliubov quasiparticle has the following form:

$$ \hat{\beta}^{\dagger}_{{\mathbf{k}},n,\uparrow}=u_{f,n}({\mathbf{k}})f^{\dagger}_{{\mathbf{k}},\uparrow}+u_{c,n}({\mathbf{k}})c^{\dagger}_{{\mathbf{k}},\uparrow}+v_{f,n}({\mathbf{k}})f_{-{\mathbf{k}},\downarrow}+v_{c,n}({\mathbf{k}})c_{-{\mathbf{k}},\downarrow}\,, $$

in which $c^{\dagger}$ and $f^{\dagger}$ stand for the fermion creation operator for TPLO and MLWF, respectively. We note that due to the $S_{z}$ conservation, $\hat{\beta}^{\dagger}$ operators will only contain the creation operators of the spin-up states, and annihilation operators of the spin-down states. The Bogoliubov amplitudes $u,v$ satisfy the normalization condition:

$$ 1=\sum_{\alpha=c,f}u^{*}_{\alpha,n}({\mathbf{k}})u_{\alpha,n}({\mathbf{k}})+\sum_{\alpha=c,f}v^{*}_{\alpha,n}({\mathbf{k}})v_{\alpha,n}({\mathbf{k}})\,. $$

Since the TPLO cannot be considered as a localized orbital, the natural choice for defining the Berry connection of the BdG states is the plane wave basis. In this basis, the quasiparticle operator in Eq. (S39) can be rewritten as:

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\beta}^{\dagger}_{{\mathbf{k}},n,\uparrow}= \displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{Q}}\left[c^{\dagger}_{{\mathbf{k}}-\mathbf{Q},\uparrow}\left(u_{f,n}({\mathbf{k}})\tilde{u}^{(\uparrow)}_{\mathbf{Q},f}({\mathbf{k}})+u_{c,n}({\mathbf{k}})\tilde{u}^{(\uparrow)}_{\mathbf{Q},c}({\mathbf{k}})\right)+c_{-{\mathbf{k}}-\mathbf{Q},\downarrow}\left(v_{f,n}({\mathbf{k}})\tilde{u}^{(\downarrow)*}_{\mathbf{Q},f}(-{\mathbf{k}})+v_{c,n}({\mathbf{k}})\tilde{u}^{(\downarrow)*}_{\mathbf{Q},c}(-{\mathbf{k}})\right)\right]\,, $$

in which $c^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{Q},\sigma}$ creates a plane wave with wave vector ${\mathbf{k}}-\mathbf{Q}$ in the spin-valley sector $\sigma$ . As such, an off-diagonal (non-Abelian) Berry connection of BdG states can be defined in the following form:

$$ \displaystyle\left[\exp\left(i\mathbf{A}({\mathbf{k}})\cdot d{\mathbf{k}}\right)\right]_{mn} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{Q}}\left(u^{*}_{f,n}({\mathbf{k}})\tilde{u}^{(\uparrow)*}_{\mathbf{Q},f}({\mathbf{k}})+u^{*}_{c,n}({\mathbf{k}})\tilde{u}^{(\uparrow)*}_{\mathbf{Q},c}({\mathbf{k}})\right)\left(u_{f,n}({\mathbf{k}}+d{\mathbf{k}})\tilde{u}^{(\uparrow)}_{\mathbf{Q},f}({\mathbf{k}}+d{\mathbf{k}})+u_{c,n}({\mathbf{k}}+d{\mathbf{k}})\tilde{u}^{(\uparrow)}_{\mathbf{Q},c}({\mathbf{k}}+d{\mathbf{k}})\right) \displaystyle+\left(v^{*}_{f,n}({\mathbf{k}})\tilde{u}^{(\downarrow)}_{\mathbf{Q},f}(-{\mathbf{k}})+v^{*}_{c,n}({\mathbf{k}})\tilde{u}^{(\downarrow)}_{\mathbf{Q},c}(-{\mathbf{k}})\right)\left(v_{f,n}({\mathbf{k}}+d{\mathbf{k}})\tilde{u}^{(\downarrow)*}_{\mathbf{Q},f}(-{\mathbf{k}}-d{\mathbf{k}})+v_{c,n}({\mathbf{k}}+d{\mathbf{k}})\tilde{u}^{(\downarrow)*}_{\mathbf{Q},c}(-{\mathbf{k}}-d{\mathbf{k}})\right)\,. $$

Accordingly, a Wilson loop can be defined as the path order integral of the non-Abelian connection along a given direction. For example, we can choose the Wilson loop contour along $\mathbf{b}_{2}$ with fixed value of $k_{1}$ :

$$ W(k_{1})=\mathcal{P}\exp\left(i\int_{0}^{2\pi}dk_{2}\,A_{2}({\mathbf{k}})\right)\approx\prod_{K_{2}=0}^{L_{2}-1}\exp\left[i\mathbf{A}\left(\frac{k_{1}}{2\pi}\mathbf{b}_{1}+\frac{K_{2}}{L_{2}}\mathbf{b_{2}}\right)\cdot\frac{\mathbf{b}_{2}}{L}\right]\,, $$

which is a unitary matrix. Its eigenvalues $\lambda_{j}(k_{1})=e^{i\theta_{j}(k_{1})}$ and its determinant are gauge invariant quantities, which carry important information about the topology of the Bogoliubov quasiparticles.

Since the the TPLO itself is topological obstructed, the determination of the topology of the BdG state might be affect. Therefore, a reasonable “reference point”, which corresponds to the case in the absence of Cooper pairing, has to be considered. Here, we consider the case with both bands fully filled and no pairing terms as the reference state. This state is sketched in Fig. S4(a), where the solid and dashed lines stand for the particle and hole sectors of the BdG bands. The phase of $\det W(k_{1})$ computed from the top two bands is shown in Fig. S4(b). The non-vanishing winding number $\mathcal{C}=-2$ is clearly inherited from the non-interacting band structure. When the electrons form Cooper pairs, the particle and hole sectors will be “hybridized”, as sketched in Fig. S4(c). When the pairing function form ${}^{1}E$ or ${}^{2}E$ representations of $C_{3}$ , the corresponding plots of $\det W(k_{1})$ are shown in Figs. S4(d-e), respectively. Here, we have used the order parameter amplitude $\Delta/W\approx 0.15$ . Compared to their counterparts without Cooper pairing, the Wilson loop winding number changes by $\Delta\mathcal{C}=\pm 2$ in these two cases, which is indeed a hallmark of $d\pm id$ pairing symmetry.

The subtraction of winding numbers of “normal state” can be also considered from another perspective. When we truncate the fully-filled remote bands of the continuum model during the projection procedure, these bands will carry the opposite winding number as the two active bands. In the presence of pairing order parameter, these bands will still remain filled. Subtracting the winding numbers of the normal state from the superconducting state is equivalent to adding the total winding number of all the filled bands. Therefore, the Chern number change $\Delta\mathcal{C}=\pm 2$ is indeed the topological index of the superconducting state with all bands considered.

The generalization to the two orbital model with Chern numbers $\mathcal{C}=(-1,+1)$ is straightforward. In such case, the Wilson loops can be computed similarly, by simply replacing the plane wave decomposition of MLWF and the TPLO with their counterparts for the two exponentially localized orbitals. Fig. S5 shows the winding of $\det W(k_{1})$ with three types of order parameters with different $C_{3}$ irreps. In particular, ${}^{1,2}E$ irreps can lead to topological superconductors with Chern number $\mathcal{C}=\pm 1$ .

Since the effective model in the parameter regime with $\mathcal{C}=(-1,+1)$ is a legitimate tight-binding model, we are also able to perform an open boundary condition calculation for these Bogoliubov quasiparticles. For three types of pairing order parameters, the open boundary condition spectra are shown Fig. S6. Here we computed the open boundary Bogoliubov spectra using particle-hole redundant representation, and the number of edge modes on each edge is twice the Chern number suggested by the Wilson loop winding number.

## Abstract

During the spring of 2022, an archaeo-metallurgical survey was conducted by the Beijing University of

Science and Technology at the Wangxiangping site in Daye County. This subsequent testing excavation

uncovered pottery and metal smelting relics from the Shang and Zhou dynasties. Charcoal samples

extracted from the third stratification can be dated using 14C to as early as the late Shang Dynasty. The

SEM-EDS method was employed to analyze the metallurgical relics found in each stratification layer of

the site. The analysis revealed that pure copper smelting and tin bronze smelting activities coexisted at

this location. Research results suggest that secondary copper oxide ore was used for reduction smelting,

resulting in the production of red copper and high-grade 'white' matte. Additionally, tin ore was

incorporated to create bronze, with tin serving as the alloy composition. However, no residual artifacts

from casting activities were discovered. The survey and detection analysis conducted at this site offer

significant evidence and data supporting further research into copper smelting activities in the Daye area

during the Shang and Zhou dynasties.

## Introduction

The Daye area in Hubei is abundant in copper, lead, and other mineral resources, making it well-known for

its mining and smelting activities during the Bronze Age. Previous research has demonstrated that the area and its surroundings contain numerous diverse smelting sites. Notable examples include the ancient

Tonglüshan copper mine smelting site and related mining and smelting surveys. Research indicates that mining at Daye Tonglüshan evolved from open-pit to underground operations during the Shang and Zhou

periods[1]. Studies on the nearby Xianglushan site have suggested that it refined antimony bronze, leadtin bronze, and red copper, among other technologies[2, 3]. Numerous smelting sites have also been

reported in surrounding areas such as Yangxin Dalupu site[4], Jiangxi Ruichang Tongling area[5], and Anhui Zongyang area[6]. Recent work has revealed numerous Shangzhou lead smelting sites in the Yangxin area[7], which have introduced new methods for studying mining and smelting sites, such as

identifying micro-slag at casting locations[8]. Research on mining and smelting sites has covered an extensive geographical range, with numerous investigations and excavations conducted in locations

such as Oman, the Sinai Peninsula, the Arab Valley, Cyprus, the Balkan Peninsula, the Danube River middle reaches region, the Austrian Alps, the Spanish Rio Tinto mining area, Thailand Banqing, and South

America's Peru. In-depth studies have also been carried out at sites like Shiqmim in southern Israel[9], the Feynan site in Jordan[10], and the Massa Marittima site in southern Tuscany, Italy[11].

On February 4th, 2022, the Beijing University of Science and Technology carried out a special

investigation of mining and metallurgical sites in the Daye area. The investigation primarily focused on understanding the occurrence and distribution of mining and metallurgical remains, as well as the scale

and characteristics of smelting activities in the region. The WXP (Wangxingping for short) site, discovered

during the survey, is an exemplary representation of early smelting activities in the area. 14C dating of a

charcoal sample taken from the site's bottom layer (the ③ layer) places it in the late Shang Dynasty period. This report offers valuable insights into local smelting sites from the late Shang Dynasty to the early

## The Background of the Site and Result

The WXP (Wangxiangdun) site is situated 50 meters southeast of Xiashoupu Bay in Dazhuang Village,

Liurenba Town, Daye County, Huangshi City, Hubei Province. According to the 3rd national official archaeological survey, the settlement site is thought to belong to the Western Zhou period. The WXP site

is located 300 meters southeast of Dazhuangwu in Dongshan Village, Liurenba Town, and spans an area of approximately 12,000 square meters with an archaeological stratigraphy thickness of 1.5-2 meters.

The pottery found at the site is predominantly yellow-brown temperless pottery, accompanied by red sand tempered pottery. Decorative elements on the pottery include rope patterns and string patterns featured

on li-tripods, yan-steamers, dou-stemmed bowls, and guan-jars[12].

## The Straitification Structure and Radiocarbon Dating Result

During this survey, a new profile was discovered at the mountain top terraces. The profile faces west and spans a width of 240cm. It can be divided into three layers:

1. The first layer ①, found below the surface soil, is the disturbance layer. It is 20-30cm thick and

consists of gray-brown soil with fine sand particles. The soil in this layer is relatively loose. 2. The second layer ② is the cultural layer, which is 70-110cm thick. It contains fine sand particles within

blue-gray clay. The color is lighter than that of the first layer, and it includes furnace slag, charcoal shavings, pottery fragments, and other cultural artifacts.

3. The third layer ③ is another cultural layer, mainly composed of yellow clay with a thickness of 15-

30cm. This layer contains sandstone red pottery, sandstone gray pottery, furnace slag, charcoal

## The Sampling Strategy and Investment Methods

In smelting sites, various relics and artifacts can be used to study smelting technology. One of the easiest to obtain is slag, the waste product created during smelting. In copper smelting activities, slag production is a core process. Slag is discharged from the furnace in a molten state at smelting temperatures and

solidifies into a dense solid, permanently sealing the metallurgical reaction information within. The properties of slag directly affect the success of the smelting process. As a result, detecting and analyzing slag can help reveal ancient copper smelting technology. At the WXP site, the metallurgical content was investigated through surface and section surveys. The smelting slag found neither accumulated nor

distributed sparsely, and the quantity was small. The slag blocks came in various shapes and had mostly dark gray surfaces. The size of the slag bodies ranged from 2–5 cm in length and width, and some larger pieces were approximately 10 cm in length and width, with a thickness of 1-2.5 cm. The slag was relatively small and did not accumulate. To better understand the metallurgical content of the WXP site,

10 samples were selected for testing.

As shown in Fig. 4, there is no significant difference in color between the slag samples from the WXP site. The lighter portions of the slag may be due to the burial environment and difficulties in external cleaning. Most of the slag is small in size, with no large blocks of slag residue present at the site. The length of

most slag pieces is about 10cm. The fluidity of most slag is poor, and some slag samples have many pores, The sample WXP③-02 has more pores and is lighter. Overall, the slag collected from the surface has lower viscosity than the slag unearthed from the cultural layer, and its density is also higher. The stratum slag is more irregular due to its poor fluidity, its surface is more uneven, and it adheres to more heat-

treated sandy soil and the like. There are a small number of slag pieces with traces of having flowed out, such as smelting slag collected from the surface. It is not difficult to find this kind of slag in the field, as it varies in characteristics like color, appearance, texture, and specific gravity. Fortunately, almost all ancient metallurgical slags are ferrous silicates, whether they are by-products of iron or non-ferrous metal

production. This fact helps in identifying and distinguishing them from non-metallurgical slags found on site.

In addition to iron and silicon as the main components, the slag composition contains relatively high

As illustrated in these Fig. 5–6, most of the slag falls within the ideal melting area of the ternary phase diagram[15]. ## Discussion

## The Technology of Smelting

Compared to the slag composition of furnace slag at locations such as Sifangtang, Donglike, and

Nonghang in the Daye area, the average aluminum content of the slag from WXP site and Tonglüshan site is half of the average composition of the aforementioned sites. This difference may be attributed to the longer duration of mining in the Tonglüshan mining area, leading to the presence of more sulfide ores or vein components when mining deep oxidized ore beds, or perhaps due to Tonglüshan using lowergrade copper ore.

The average copper content of the WXP site is 0.9%. Analyzing the properties of smelting slag by examining metal particles such as red copper particles and white bronze particles reveals that this type of

red copper smelting slag is all reduction slag smelted using the direct method. The slag matrix contains a large amount of ferrous olivine. Some slag matrices contain a small amount of floating Shi, which are common by-products in the smelting process.

The smelting process follows an oxide ore-copper technology type, consistent with various locations in Tonglüshan. It may be determined according to different regions that the use of ores with different grades contains some sulfide copper metal particles that may be oxidized ores containing some sulfide ores.

Tin bronze alloy technology can be traced back to various sites around WXP, including the Daye

Xianglushan site[3], Anhui Tongling Shigudun[17] and Xiajiadun sites[18]. Bronze alloy slag from the Western Zhou period has been found at all these sites, indicating that bronze alloy smelting technology was present in the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River during the Shang and Zhou dynasties. This suggests a relatively broad distribution of this technology. Yangxin County, a well-known neighboring county, has numerous cultural relics from the Shang and Zhou dynasties, such as bronze Nao-bells, Ge-dagger-axes, bronze axes, and other bronze artifacts. These items are mainly housed in the Yangxin County Museum, indicating that the region had a substantial bronze smelting and casting industry during the Shang and Zhou periods. An earlier instance of this is the Yangxin Dalupu site, where bronze smelting and casting relics dating back to the end of the Neolithic period have been found. Alloy

bronze pieces were discovered during the Hou Shijiahe culture period at the Yangxin Dalupu site[4]. However, large-scale evidence of this technological advancement has not been uncovered yet. The Provenance of Copper Raw Material

Cultural relics survey data indicate that during the Shang and Zhou dynasties, the central government of

China placed great importance on the southeastern Hubei region's management. The region, where the Daye WXP site is located, is a crucial large-scale mining area in the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River, abundant with copper-iron-gold-lead and other mineral resources. The Tongshankou copper mine, a large copper mining area, is less than 5 kilometers away from the WXP site. The characteristics of mineral resources in the Daye area suggest that there are indeed numerous copper polymetallic ore spots in this region. In the Jiguanzui-Longjiaoshan copper polymetallic survey area within Daye City, over ten copper-lead-zinc-molybdenum-iron ore deposits and more than 50 physical and chemical exploration anomalies have been identified. The Shizishan mining area, adjacent to the

Tongshankou Copper Mine, primarily consists of the N1 and N2 ore bodies. The upper part of the N1 ore body is mostly made up of oxidized or mixed ore, with a brown honeycomb-shaped, loose soil-like coppercontaining iron cap and a copper grade ranging from 0.7–6.2%. The N2 ore body primarily contains two types of ores: oxidized ore and primary ore, with an average copper grade of 2.6%. Oxidized ore accounts for 82.7% of the N2 ore body[19]. The vertical depth of the ore body reaches − 408.5 meters, with the main ore volume found between − 50 and − 150 meters. The deposit is mainly controlled by the contact zone, belonging to a typical medium-temperature hydrothermal alteration skarn polymetallic copper deposit[20]. In 1961, a large deposit was discovered nearby, identified as a contact alteration skarn type

deposit[21].

The Tongshankou mining area is situated approximately 18 kilometers southwest of Daye County in Hubei Province. It is located on the eastern side of the northern part of the Dongting Depression, between the Jiangnan Ancient Land and Huaiyang Shield. The area lies on the favorable polymetallic mineralization belt extending in the Daye-Tongshankou northeast direction.

The main minerals in the ore include chalcopyrite and pyrite, with magnetite, chalcocite, sphalerite, and galena also present in smaller amounts. The industrial reserves of copper mines in Copper Mine

Mountain, Bangke Mountain, and Shizishan all exceed 500 thousand tons[20]. The Provenance of Tin Raw Material

There have been no reports of tin ore exploration in Hubei Province, particularly in the southeastern Hubei region. Consequently, the Daye area, where the WXP site is located, lacks tin resources and depends on imports from other regions. If this type of slag is traced back to the smelting process, the most probable process, given the characteristics of this smelting product, would involve first using copper oxide ore with high iron content (in which some copper or iron sulfide minerals remain) for reduction smelting. Near the end of smelting, most slag is removed (i.e., pure copper smelting slag), and tin material is added to the furnace to continue reduction smelting. Finally, a small amount of slag containing tin bronze particles is discharged to obtain bronze with tin as the main alloying element. Tin minerals with higher copper and iron content may be residues of stannite desulfurization and cassiterite dehydration, respectively, and

could serve as indicators of tin ore origin. Similar signs have been found at the Chenjiashan site in Zongyang, Anhui Province. The northern part of Jiangxi, adjacent to eastern Hubei, has been identified as a tin-producing region along the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River. This area offers strong

evidence in terms of geographical location and metallurgical archaeological background of early sites. Numerous renowned mining sites are present, with four sites distributed across De'an, Fuliang, Yongxiu, and Yifeng-Shanggao counties[22]. Besides the discovery of minerals such as cassiterite (SnO2) and

stannite (Cu2FeSnS4), Varlamoffite (Sn-Fe)(O-OH)2 has also been identified numerous times[23]. This

mineral is found in the oxidized zone of skarn iron-copper deposits, medium-low temperature cassiterite sulfide deposits, and tin-containing skarn positive contact zones. Based on the above observations, the source of tin ore used in tin bronze smelting sites, such as the Yujia'ao site in eastern Hubei, could be traced to the Jiangxi tin ore area. However, further archaeological investigations, exploration, and excavation work are required to confirm this. Technology of Copper Smelting Industry during the Shang and Zhou Dynasties at Hubei

During the Shang and Zhou dynasties, the characteristics of the copper smelting industry in Hubei can be discussed based on the findings from the Daye WXP and Daye Xianglushan sites. These sites share

similarities in terms of unearthed relics and are mainly concentrated during the late Shang-Western Zhou period. This suggests that mining and smelting activities were prevalent in the local area at that time, with most sites being located on the outer edge of valleys near mountains and water sources. These areas provided not only convenient transportation resources but also met the necessary requirements for water and fuel for smelting operations.

Moreover, the management of mining and metallurgy during that time appeared to be relatively loose, with no large-scale unified mining and smelting activities occurring in major mines. However, subsequent periods saw a more stringent management approach to mining and metallurgy at sites such as

Tonglüshan in Daye. The investigation of the Daye WXP site and analysis of metallurgical technology revealed a well-preserved site with clear evidence of metallurgical processes and diverse technical types. This makes the site suitable for further investigation and excavation, as well as expanding the exploration of surrounding sites. Sites like WXP contribute to our understanding of the metallurgical industrial production in Hubei during the Shang and Zhou dynasties. However, it is important to note that this information comes from a single site, and further site investigations are needed to reveal a comprehensive picture of the copper smelting industry in southeastern Hubei during that time.

## Conclusion

The investigation and analysis of mining and metallurgy sites and their associated metallurgical technology have highlighted the importance of the Daye WXP site in Hubei during the Shang and Zhou

dynasties. The stratigraphic profile 14C chronology analysis indicates that the site dates back to the late Shang Dynasty and has a significant time span. Numerous living relics have been discovered at the site, and the slag extracted from the cultural layer and collected from the surface demonstrates that the

metallurgical technology of this site consisted of both copper smelting and tin bronze alloying. This indicates the presence of copper metallurgy activities in Daye during that period.

## Abstract

Although sports mouthguards (MGs) are mandatory in some contact sports, the use of conventional fabricated materials for making MGs is time-consuming and lacks precision, limiting their widespread application. In this study, we compared mouthguards designed using digital software with conventional ones. The conventional mouthguards were categorized into two types: those constructed from a poly-(ethylene vinyl acetate)-base material, and those constructed from MG21, a polyolefin-base material. The shock absorption and durability were assessed through a free-falling steel ball test and a fatigue test. The durability of the MGs was evaluated by measuring the retention force in the inner layer and deviations at consistent points on the outer layer during various fatigue test stages. Additively manufactured samples showed superior shock absorption performance, except for the double-layer samples with an inner layer of Shore A hardness 95. All single-layer additively manufactured MGs were damaged during the mid-fatigue test stage, while both double-layer additively manufactured and conventional MGs remained undamaged. Throughout all fatigue test stages, the retention force of double-layer additively manufactured MGs was significantly lower than that of conventional MGs. However, the retention force of double-layer additively manufactured samples with an inner layer of Shore A hardness 70 (D-A70) was superior to the average of all MGs in the wet condition, which was 6.4 ± 2.5 N in the previous study. The results of this study demonstrated the benefits of a hybrid design of hard and soft materials, particularly the promising combination of D-A70, which exhibited comparable shock absorption and durability to conventional MGs.

## 1. Introduction

A sports mouthguard (MG) is essential for protecting the hard and soft tissues of the oral cavity, including teeth and gums, from impact during athletic activities. The World Dental Federation emphasizes the importance of custommade sports MGs in preventing trauma.1 In certain contact sports, such as boxing, MGs usage is mandatory because they reduce the risk of traumatic dental injuries and brain concussions, as demonstrated by extensive research.2-8

Despite their importance, creating a comfortable and durable MG is a complex challenge. The fabrication process, particularly the thermoforming phase, often results in diminished thickness around the anterior teeth, which can affect both comfort and protection.9 Additionally, each MG must be tailored to fit comfortably, adding to the complexity of the design.

The emergence of three-dimensional (3D) digital design and additive manufacturing process, known for its customization, rapid production, and cost-efficiency, has attracted substantial interest. Prior studies have validated its safety and effectiveness,10-13 suggesting a promising future for additively manufactured sports MGs.

In 2020, Li et al. published an extensive exposition of the digital design and manufacturing of sports MGs.14

By implementing a semi-digital workflow, Hada et al. examined how temperature fluctuations affected the material properties of sports MGs.15 After investigating various materials, Sousa et al.16 found that three additively manufactured materials—recycled polylactic acid (rPLA), polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA), and high-impact polystyrene (HIPS)—outperformed a conventional material, poly-(ethylene vinyl acetate) (EVA) in the shock absorption experiment. A study by Pinho et al.17 demonstrated increased elasticity and resistance in aged sandwich samples.

The processes are categorized into International Organization for Standardization/American Society for Testing and Materials (ISO/ASTM) process classes in medical applications of additively manufactured powder bed fusion, material extrusion, vat photopolymerization, material jetting, binder jetting, sheet lamination, and directed energy deposition.18 The Polyjet process (Stratasys Ltd., Rehovot, Israel), a revolutionary multi-material jetting process, was widely applied for higher precision and printing speed, the ability to print multiple materials, and hands-free removal of support structure.19

Materials of acrylate-base photoinitiator composites (Agilus, Vero, digital poly-(acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene) [D-ABS]) are preferred for additively manufactured MGs due to their excellent protection capability, which is the

most critical ability of MG. These materials are competitive with those of conventional fabricated materials like EVA and polyolefin (PO).20,21 It has been demonstrated that incorporating a hard insert within a conventional material can significantly enhance the protection capability.22

While the shock absorption and dispersion properties of additively manufactured MGs have been extensively studied, there is a need for more focused research on their durability, especially considering the intermittent occlusal forces during athletic activities.21 Durability is another crucial factor for the long-term, effective, and safe use of MGs. The resistance to surface wear and deformation from continuous use has been evaluated for conventional MG materials,23 but the durability of additively manufactured MGs requires further investigation. Hard occlusal surfaces in devices such as night guards, which prevent bruxism, have been shown to improve durability and reduce wear.24

This study aimed to assess the effectiveness of combining hard and soft materials in additively manufactured MGs to enhance shock absorption and dispersion properties in simulated oral environments. Additionally, it evaluated the durability, retention force, and morphological changes of these MGs, particularly in response to the effects of intermittent occlusal forces on their surfaces in simulated oral environments.

The composites were blended in their liquid state before the printing process.25 Single-layer samples were specified as having a diameter of 50 mm and a thickness of 3 mm. Double-layer samples consist of a 0.5 mm thick hard layer of D-ABS and a 2.5 mm thick, soft layer of Agilus or/and Vero composites (A30- 95), designated as D-A30 through D-A95, respectively (Figure 1). Material samples were printed by a J850 Digital Anatomy 3D printer (Stratasys Ltd., Rehovot, Israel) with a dual-head liquid output. Conventional MG sheets made of PO-base material (MG21; CGK, Hiroshima, Japan) and EVA-base material (Erkoflex [ERK]; Erkodent Erich Kopp GmbH, Pfalzgrafenweiler, Germany) were molded for comparison. Schewe et al. explored the shock absorption of photoinitiators, but did not clarify the specific requirements for designing MGs with a thickness of 2–4 mm.37 MGs thicker than 4 mm may cause joint discomfort due to the 2–4 mm freeway space in the mouth.38 Previous studies have not extensively considered the effects of the oral environment, such as temperature and humidity.21,37 Most experiments have been executed at room temperature and humidity because the conditions follow international standards, and are globally applicable.39 In Tun et al.’s study,21 the shock absorption rate of Agilus30 at room temperature was 26.9%, but it increased to 65.3% in this study. As with Compo50, Agilus50 (A50) showed an increased absorption rate from 44.8% at room temperature and humidity to 63.3% under simulated oral conditions. In contrast, conventional MG materials, ERK and MG21, demonstrated consistent absorption rates of around 43.5% and 41.8% at room temperature, and approximately 45.5% and 44.5% under simulated oral conditions. Our study demonstrated that additively manufactured material samples had an improvement in shock absorption in a simulated oral environment.

Both layer design and Shore A hardness affect shock absorption properties. The free-falling steel ball test indicated layered design was more influential than hardness of materials, as demonstrated by statistical significance between hardness-paired material samples (Figure 7). The MIF-t approximation function for single-layer samples suggested a more complex relationship, with an additional peak in growth after A70 samples, encouraging further investigation (Figure 9).

Our research confirmed that double-layer additively manufactured MG samples were preferred to single-layer MG samples, as the single-layer MG samples can be damaged at fatigue tests. Despite the superior shock absorption ability of single-layer additively manufactured samples, their propensity to crack during cycle-loading fatigue tests suggests that single-layer designs are not feasible for future use. Double-layer additively manufactured MG samples exhibited superior shock absorption than conventionally fabricated MG samples ERK and MG21, except for the type of D-A95 samples. In addition, double-layer additively manufactured materials (D-A50, D-A60, D-A70) had the same MIF-t values as conventional materials.

Our research also proved that fabricating inconsistencies affected the retention force of conventionally fabricated MG samples. However, additively manufactured MG samples have manufacturing consistencies, superior shock absorption, and acceptable durability, providing more consistent, standardized, and reliable safety protection.

In addition to shock absorption, a MG must ensure a sufficient retention force to avoid dislocation during rapid movement. Previous research30 indicated that the average retention force of conventionally fabricated MGs was 6.4 ± 2.5 N in wet conditions. This value was exceeded only by D-A70 type of MG samples when without any use. The MG sample is expected to have more specialized applications for individuals involved in fast-moving contact sports, such as football players and boxers.

According to the evaluation of retention force and RMS, only MG21 samples showed a statistical significance of a larger retention force with a smaller RMS deviation in fatigue tests (Tables 5 and 6). However, previous studies suggest that the MG retention force decreases with continued use.40 MGs initially increase or stand the retention force before decreasing it. This may be conducive to the preparation of MG samples in future clinical applications. Further research is necessary to determine the most appropriate load preparation for MGs during fatigue tests.

There are some limitations in our study. We excluded certain values due to similar shock absorption results between the intermediate Shore A hardness number of additively manufactured material samples. Besides, the unsatisfactory results of the shock absorption tests conducted in MIF-t on D-A85 and D-A95 types of material samples removed the need for further durability tests, potentially resulting in a data exclusion. Biocompatibility is another consideration. Agilus series materials have already been applied in several medical devices, including stethoscopes41 and eye gear with prescription glasses,42 and the same type of materials are being employed in this study. However, little is known about the biocompatibility of these materials. Despite these limitations, the findings of this study may contribute to MG enhancement as a medical device in the future.

## 5. Conclusion

In this study, additively manufactured material samples (except for D-A95) made by Agilus, Vero, and D-ABS performed better in shock absorption than conventional material samples ERK and MG21 in simulated oral environments, with additively manufactured single-layer MG samples and specific types of double-layer MG samples (D-A50, D-A60, D-A70) demonstrating the same arrival time of maximum impact force (MIF-t) as conventionally fabricated MGs.

Moreover, this study provides insights into the durability and retention forces of additively manufactured MG samples, indicating that single-layer additively manufactured MG samples are less durable, but highlighting the benefits of utilizing hard materials on occlusal surfaces and effective shock absorption capabilities
